newsitem.title: EL SALVADOR: El Salvador is a nation reborn five years after war.
newsitem.headline: El Salvador is a nation reborn five years after war.

text.p: El Salvador celebrates five years of peace on Thursday having risen from the most brutal of Central America's bloody civil wars to become a nation reborn.

Peaceful elections, respect for human rights, and a booming economy now mark a nation torn by fighting between leftist rebels and a right-wing government during the 1980s -- a Cold War battleground played out in a backward nation roughly the size of the U.S. state of Massachussetts.
"It's no longer the army that rules around here," said Ruben Zamora, a leftist politician and former presidential candidate.

An estimated 75,000 Salvadorans died in 12 years of war, with the later years a bloody stalemate between the 8,000 rebels who would not give in and the 60,000-strong army, heavily armed and financed by the United States.

The war ended on Jan. 16, 1992, when the government of former President Alfredo Cristiani and guerrillas of the Farabundo Marti National Liberation Front (FMLN) signed a peace treaty at Chapultepec Castle in Mexico City.

"Most (of the peace accords) have been complied with, so what we're looking for is how to handle the job we have ahead," Alvaro de Soto, a top United Nations official helping oversee the peace accords, told reporters after meeting with President Armando Calderon Sol on Wednesday.
Today the FMLN is a legal political party, fighting it out with the ruling, right-wing ARENA party in the halls of Congress instead of the war zones of the countryside.

A wave of revenge killings in the countryside that immediately followed peace has subsided and political violence is relatively rare, unlike in nearby Nicaragua, where former combatants rearmed themselves to address grievances after eight years of civil war ended there in 1990.

The strength of the FMLN also allowed El Salvador to end the fighting quickly after the end of the Cold War, while neighbouring Guatemala only last month signed a peace agreement ending 36 years of conflict.
"The spirit of reconciliation gets lost sometimes, but it is always recovered," Victoria de Aviles, the country's highly regarded human rights prosecutor, told reporters.

In another contrast to Nicaragua, El Salvador also has become something of a economic power in the region, regularly posting annual gross domestic product growth rates of 4 percent to 5 percent, among the highest in Latin America.

As during the war, coffee remains the main export, but the service and banking sectors flourished since the war's end, and a booming industrial free zone became a major attraction for foreign investors, mostly from South Korea and Taiwan.

But more than half of El Salvador's 5.7 million people remain in poverty, and the macroeconomic success has yet to trickle down, triggering some to warn that the country's troubles may not be all in the past.
"New conditions to construct democracy in El Salvador have been created, but there is still a lack of economic and social factors," said Salvador Sanchez, a leader in the FMLN party.

Sanchez also said he was concerned about a the government's foot-dragging on recommendations by a U.N. "truth commission," which rocked the government in 1993 when it issued a report on wartime human rights abuses, blaming the army for the worst of the atrocities.
The truth commission made recommendations on how to preserve public security and human rights that have not been complied with, de Soto said.
De Soto also said the government has not yet to meet certain aspects of the peace accords such as distribution of land to former rebels and programmes to help them return to civilian life.

"The next five years present us Salvadorans with the challenge of sitting down and resolving the problems that remain," said Zamora, the leftist politician. "If we don't do it we're going to take a step backward."
